thread_analysis.thread_summary: [COMPANY] requests a Bluetooth SIG certification quote for a Volvo-destined automotive DA module (UXC), to be registered by combining the module's own RF/RF PHY test results with an existing Qualcomm Controller-layer QDID. The thread covers a Power Class compatibility requirement between the existing QDID and the module's actual transmit power, a follow-up finding that a Subset-ID-based workaround for a Power Class mismatch no longer works for new registrations after a July 1 Consistency Check change, a requirement to separately test any customer-customized version of the chipset vendor's stock Profile implementation with an early inter-layer consistency simulation, and a broader compliance point that Bluetooth SIG registration of just the embedded module may not be sufficient if the final product (the vehicle) is the one that should formally be registered.
all_questions_found: Can the customer's module be registered by combining its own RF/RF PHY test Pass report with an existing Qualcomm Controller-layer QDID, and what Power Class compatibility does that require?

If the module's LE-mode transmit power is below the threshold required by the existing QDID's registered Power Class, what alternatives are available -- a different already-registered Controller stack, or a vendor-issued updated registration?
Does the test execution split between two labs (full RF items and RF PHY 1M mode at one lab, remaining RF PHY items at another) apply to this project?
Can an existing Component registration's Subset ID still be Included in a new registration, given that inter-layer Consistency Checking became stricter since July 1?
If the chipset vendor creates a new Subset ID with the Power Class capability removed, will that Subset ID be Includable in this new registration?
If the customer customizes the chipset vendor's stock Bluetooth Profile implementation, does that customized Profile need to be separately tested?
Can an early simulation be run to confirm the test results and the Host QDID will not produce an inter-layer inconsistency (Invalid=0) before committing to full testing?
Can the DUT modification documentation needed for RF/RF PHY testing be provided ahead of time?

Since Bluetooth certification properly registers a final product, does registering only the embedded module satisfy Bluetooth SIG requirements, or does the vehicle itself need to be registered as the final product?
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The thread covers Power Class compatibility between an Included Controller-layer QDID and a module's actual transmit power range, the post-July-1 limitation that an existing registration's Subset ID cannot be Included in a new registration (closing off a previously-viable workaround for a Power Class mismatch), the need to separately test a customer-customized version of a chipset vendor's stock Profile rather than relying on the vendor's own test evidence, an early inter-layer consistency simulation service to de-risk a custom-Profile registration before committing to full testing, and the broader principle that Bluetooth SIG registration is meant to cover a product's final, as-sold form -- meaning registering an embedded automotive module alone may not satisfy the requirement if the vehicle itself is the actual end product.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: An existing Controller-layer QDID can only be combined with a module's own RF/RF PHY evidence if the module's actual transmit power falls within the Power Class the QDID is registered under; if it does not, the only viable paths are referencing a different already-registered Controller stack with the matching Class, or having the chip vendor issue an updated registration with the needed Class removed -- a Subset-ID-based shortcut for this mismatch is no longer viable for new registrations since the relevant Consistency Check change. When a customer customizes a chipset vendor's stock Profile implementation, the customization itself must be tested rather than relying on the vendor's own Profile test evidence, and running an early inter-layer consistency simulation against the Host QDID before full testing reduces the risk of a late-stage Invalid result. Finally, Bluetooth SIG registration is meant to apply to the actual final product as sold; an embedded automotive module being registered on its own does not necessarily satisfy this if the vehicle itself is the product ultimately reaching the market, though resolving this is the customer's (and their OEM's) decision to make.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: Combining the module's RF/RF PHY evidence with a Controller QDID whose registered Power Class doesn't match the module's actual transmit power would create an inter-layer inconsistency that prevents the registration from completing. Attempting to rely on a Subset-ID workaround for this mismatch would similarly fail to register, since Subset IDs are not Includable in new registrations under the current Consistency Check. Treating a customer-customized Profile as already covered by the chipset vendor's own test evidence, without separately testing the customization, risks an invalid or incomplete registration discovered only late in the process; skipping the early Invalid=0 simulation increases the risk of discovering an inter-layer inconsistency only after full testing is complete.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: When proposing to combine a module's own test evidence with an existing third-party Controller-layer QDID, verify the Power Class (or other Class-dependent capability) compatibility between the module's actual specifications and that QDID's registered configuration before quoting, and be aware that Subset-ID-based workarounds for such mismatches are no longer viable for new registrations under the current Consistency Check -- the chip vendor must issue a properly updated QDID instead. When a customer customizes a chipset vendor's stock Profile, always plan to test the customization itself and run an early inter-layer consistency simulation rather than assuming the vendor's existing test evidence covers it. For embedded automotive modules, proactively flag that the final product (the vehicle) is, in principle, what should be registered, even though resolving that is ultimately the customer's call.
